svg.aria-label: Diagram: Cloud NAT sizing and the port exhaustion failure in Google Cloud; capacity is a floor division of NAT addresses times 64,512 ports by the ports allocated per VM, giving Google's own worked figures of 1,008 VMs on one address at 64 ports, 2,016 on two, and 15 VMs when the minimum is raised to 4,096, with Private NAT dividing by twice the minimum because it allocates double for reliability; the ceilings are 300 manual or 2,500 auto-allocated addresses per gateway, 50 gateways per Cloud Router and 250 per region per network, and addresses cannot be shared between gateways, so a manually addressed gateway tops out at 19,353,600 ports; exhaustion presents as a packet drop rather than an error, surfacing as the dropped sent packets count with reason OUT_OF_RESOURCES and a boolean NAT allocation failed gauge, with dynamic allocation dropping packets while it doubles; the evidence is weakest when it matters most, because NAT logging is throttled in proportion to machine type during heavy egress and it is not possible to determine what was omitted, metrics are sampled every 60 seconds and invisible for up to 180 or 225 seconds, and the metric named Port usage actually reports the maximum number of connections from a VM to a single endpoint rather than ports consumed; and the levers are the minimum and maximum ports, both powers of two, and the timeouts, which carry a five second variance, a 15 second floor on TIME_WAIT and an extra 30 seconds before a tuple is reusable regardless
svg.title: Cloud NAT sizing: a floor division, three ceilings, and a failure that looks like packet loss
svg.text: Exhaustion is not an error. It is a dropped packet, reported late, in a log that is
throttled exactly when the trouble starts.
The capacity formula, and Google’s own worked numbers
VMs served = ⌊ (NAT addresses x 64,512) / ports per VM ⌋ — “round down … to the closest integer”.
1 address, 64 ports per VM → 1,008 VMs. 2 addresses, same 64 → 2,016 VMs.
1 address, minimum raised to 4,096 → 15 VMs. The divisor dominates, not the address count.
PRIVATE NAT divides by 2x the minimum — it “allocates double … for reliability”. A /29 gives
4 usable addresses (four are unusable), so at 1,024 ports per VM: 126 VMs, not 252.
A /28 at 64 ports reaches 6,048 VMs. One prefix bit is a 3x swing, because the usable count
is 2^(32−prefix) − 4, not 2^(32−prefix).
Three ceilings, and none of them is the port count
• ADDRESSES PER GATEWAY — 300 manual, or 2,500 auto-allocated. Manual trades headroom for
addresses you can allowlist in advance.
• GATEWAYS — 50 per Cloud Router; 5 routers per region per network, so 250 per region.
• SUBNET RANGES — 50 per gateway, when you list ranges explicitly.
“NAT IP addresses can’t be shared between NAT gateways.” So a second gateway is a second pool,
not a bigger one. A manual gateway tops out at 300 x 64,512 = 19,353,600 ports.
What exhaustion looks like: a drop, not an error
“If there aren’t enough available NAT tuples, the dropped_sent_packets_count reason is
OUT_OF_RESOURCES.” No API error. No rejected call. A packet that left and never arrived.
Gateway-level signal: nat/nat_allocation_failed, a BOOLEAN gauge — it tells you that some VM
failed to get addresses, not which one, not how badly.
The other drop reason on the same metric is ENDPOINT_INDEPENDENCE_CONFLICT — a different
fault with identical symptoms, so always read the reason label.
Dynamic allocation also drops packets WHILE it grows the allocation. Ramping up more slowly helps.
The evidence is weakest exactly when you need it
“During periods of heavy egress traffic, NAT logging is THROTTLED, proportional to the machine
type of the VM … it is NOT POSSIBLE TO DETERMINE WHAT IS OMITTED during throttling.”
Heavy egress is also when exhaustion happens. The sample thins as the incident peaks.
Metrics lag: sampled every 60 seconds, then invisible for up to 180 seconds — 225 for the
gateway-level drop count. A four-minute-old view of a one-minute problem.
AND THE NAME MISLEADS: nat/port_usage, display name “Port usage”, actually reports the
“maximum number of connections from a VM to a SINGLE internet endpoint (IP:port)”.
The levers, and the floors under them
PORTS: min is a power of 2 in 32–32,768. Max is a power of 2 in 64–65,536, default 65,536.
STATIC sizing: set the minimum EQUAL to peak usage. DYNAMIC: min below peak, max above.
Read peak over 30 days, “or another period that you think is representative”.
TIMEOUTS trade port reuse against broken flows. TCP established idle: 1,200s. TIME_WAIT: 30s
for gateways created after 30 September 2026 — check effectiveTcpTimeWaitTimeoutSec.
FLOORS: ±5s variance on every timeout; TIME_WAIT at least 15s; and “regardless of the value”
up to 30 more seconds before a tuple is reusable. Tuning below ~45s buys nothing.
Order of operations when you are short of ports: reduce demand first, then raise the minimum,
then add addresses. Google’s own wording: “before you increase the number of ports per VM,
consider other strategies for reducing port usage.” Raising the minimum shrinks VMs per address.
